title: A Reply on Single-Mindedness

blocks.text: Why Must One Be Single-Mindedly Undisturbed in Reciting the Buddha

inline.s: Q: Why must one be single-mindedly undisturbed in reciting the Buddha?

A: The study of the Buddha-Dharma is the cultivation of the mind, and its course is: the myriad thoughts returning to one (subduing afflictions); the one returning to nothing; seeing the mind and realizing the true nature (cutting off the delusions of view); cutting off afflictions (cutting off the delusions of thought); cutting off the delusions of dust and sand; partially realizing the Dharma-body; and fully realizing the fruit of Buddhahood.

[The three delusions] The delusions of view and thought, the delusions of dust and sand, and the delusion of ignorance. The delusions of view and thought are the delusions of ordinary beings. Among them, the delusion of view is delusion and error in one's views, such as the five wrong views: the view of a self, the view of extremes, the perverse view, the view of holding to [wrong] views, and the view of holding to [wrong] precepts and practices; the delusion of thought is delusion and error in one's thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt — cutting these off enables one to end birth and death and leave the three realms. The delusions of dust and sand are the delusions of bodhisattvas: in delivering sentient beings, if a bodhisattva is not versed in the countless Dharmas as numerous as dust and sand, he cannot accomplish the work of transforming sentient beings, hence they are called the delusions of dust and sand. The delusion of ignorance is the fundamental ignorance, which can obstruct the principle of the reality of the Middle Way; when it is entirely cut off, one becomes a Buddha. Among the three delusions, the delusions of view and thought are coarse, the delusions of dust and sand are middling, and ignorance is subtle. [Partially realizing the Dharma-body (fen zheng fashen)] After a bodhisattva has cut off the delusions of dust and sand, he destroys a portion of ignorance and realizes a portion of the Dharma-body; this is called a great being of the Dharma-body. From the first abiding stage up to the stage equal to Enlightenment, there are forty-one stages in all; when ignorance is entirely destroyed, one fully realizes the Dharma-body and becomes a Buddha.

The common-path teaching requires one to cut off afflictions before one can end birth and death and escape the wheel of rebirth. But the Pure Land teaching is an extremely sublime teaching: so long as one has faith and vow and holds to the name, and attains single-mindedness (the myriad thoughts returning to one), at the moment of death one can be assured of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so end birth and death and escape the wheel of rebirth.

Therefore, the World-Honored One specifically teaches in the Amitābha Sutra spoken by the Buddha: hold to the name, single-mindedly undisturbed. The sutra says: “If there are good men or good women who hear of Amitābha Buddha and hold to his name, for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, single-mindedly undisturbed, then when their life comes to an end, Amitābha Buddha with the host of holy ones appears before them; at the end of life, without a mind that is inverted, they are thereupon reborn in Amitābha Buddha's land of Ultimate Bliss.”

Master Ouyi, the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school, says in the Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sutra spoken by the Buddha: “Faith is to believe in oneself and in another, to believe in cause and in effect, in matters and in principle; the vow is to weary of the Sahā world and to yearn for Ultimate Bliss; the practice is to hold to the name, single-mindedly undisturbed.” This shows that the requirement of holding to the name is single-mindedness.

Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, says: “Single-mindedness is the ultimate destination of the pure karma and the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, one is ultimately not secure — how can students not exert themselves!” (From the Dharma Words of Master Chewu.) This shows that without attaining single-mindedness, one is ultimately not secure.

Master Lianchi, the eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school, says: “Now that one is single-mindedly undisturbed, at the moment of death the right thought gathers within and the Buddha's welcome is sensed without; casting off this reward-body, one is thereupon born in that land.” (From the Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Amitābha Sutra.) This shows that the key to ensuring rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is: at the moment of death, the right thought gathers within and the Buddha's welcome is sensed without. And to be able to accomplish “at the moment of death, the right thought gathers within and the Buddha's welcome is sensed without,” the key is precisely what Master Lianchi points out: that in daily life one can already recite the Buddha single-mindedly undisturbed (“now that one is single-mindedly undisturbed”). Therefore, the essential formula for ensuring rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is: true faith and earnest vow, single-mindedness. This is also the guiding principle of practice for a reciter of the Buddha.
Q: Please describe the state of single-mindedness.

A: Single-mindedness is when the Buddha's name in the mind is clear and distinct, neither drowsy nor scattered. In terms of the course of practice, single-mindedness has the following four levels: first, ten recitations undisturbed; second, a hundred recitations undisturbed; third, a thousand recitations undisturbed; fourth, undisturbed at any time. What is usually meant by single-mindedness refers to being undisturbed at any time. For its concrete content, see further
Awareness in Buddha-Recitation
chapter seven of the Buddha-recitation section, “The Four Levels.”

Q: The Primal Vow school says in the article “What Counts as Single-Mindedness”: “‘Single-minded’ means focused, and ‘undisturbed’ means unmixed — not mixing practices and not mixed cultivation.” This says that to recite the Buddha with focus, without mixing practices and without mixed cultivation, is to be single-mindedly undisturbed. Is this correct?

A: This statement is absurd and laughable — it shows at a glance how the Primal Vow school departs from the sutras and rebels against the Way and invents things out of nothing. Single-mindedness is the “
mindfulness without confusion”
(see further
Commentary on the Sutra Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha's Reception
) in the Xuanzang translation of the Amitābha Sutra spoken by the Buddha, the Sutra Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha's Reception; it is the “
unifying the six faculties, the pure thought
(the thought of Buddha-recitation)
in continuous succession
(not interrupted by stray thoughts)
see further
Commentary on the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Buddha-Recitation by Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta
in the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Buddha-Recitation by Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta; and it is what Master Shandao calls “
thought after thought in continuous succession”
. Master Shandao says:
“It is precisely because calling the name is easy that continued succession brings rebirth. If one is able to
continue thought after thought
, going on until the end of life, then of ten, ten will be reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred will be reborn.”
see further
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching

blocks.text: Why Is the Pure Land Teaching Called the Easy Path

inline.s: Q: Why is the Pure Land teaching called the easy path?

A: The common-path teaching requires cutting off afflictions before one can end birth and death and escape the wheel of rebirth. But the Pure Land teaching is an extremely sublime teaching: so long as one has faith and vow and holds to the name and attains single-mindedness, at the moment of death one can be assured of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so end birth and death and escape the wheel of rebirth. By comparison, the Pure Land teaching is truly, immeasurably easier. Moreover, in cultivating the common-path teaching, those who can end birth and death in this very life are after all far and few between. Those who do not end birth and death in this life enter the six realms of rebirth at death and form the enmity of three lives: because of this life's cultivation, in the next life they enjoy great wealth and honor; then, relying on that power, they commit evil, and in the life after that they fall into evil realms. By the time they can hear the Buddha-Dharma and cultivate again, who knows which eon and which life it will be! But in cultivating the Pure Land teaching, so long as one works diligently, everyone can attain single-mindedness in reciting the Buddha in this very life and be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at death. When the flower opens and one sees the Buddha, one realizes the stage of non-retrogression; on the bodhi path one only advances and never retreats until one becomes a Buddha. Therefore, the “easy” of the easy path, being spoken in contrast to the “difficult” of the common-path teaching, does not mean that the Pure Land teaching requires no earnest cultivation, and that one can casually attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. So the Buddha, in the
Sutra Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha's Reception
(the Xuanzang translation of the Amitābha Sutra spoken by the Buddha), after speaking of mindfulness without confusion (single-mindedness), again and again and repeatedly emphasizes to
practice as taught
, and clearly tells us:
so long as one practices as taught

, one is received and protected by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and one never retrogresses and quickly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. His tender concern overflows in word. The World-Honored One teaches:

“If there are pure-hearted good men or good women who hear of such inconceivable virtue of the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and of the pure Buddha-land of the land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all believe, accept, and make the vow,
practice as taught
, and be born in that Buddha-land.”
those who practice as taught

are all certain to attain non-retrogression in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all certain to be born in the pure Buddha-land of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Therefore, Śāriputra, you sentient beings should all believe, accept, and understand the words of me and the Buddhas of the ten directions; you should diligently and earnestly
practice as taught
, and harbor no doubt.”
those who practice as taught

are all certain to attain non-retrogression in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all certain to be born in the pure Buddha-land of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Therefore, Śāriputra, if there are pure-hearted good men or good women, they should all, with deep faith and understanding in the pure Buddha-land of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, make the vow to be reborn there,
and not act with indolence

“In this world of defilement and endurance, in this evil time of the five corruptions, if there are pure-hearted good men or good women who hear of such Dharmas supremely hard to believe in all the world, and can give rise to faith and understanding, receive, uphold, and expound them, and
practice as taught

, you should know that such persons are extremely rare, and that in the presence of countless Buddhas they have planted good roots. At the end of their lives they are certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and to enjoy the Mahāyāna Dharma-bliss of that pure Buddha-land adorned with manifold virtues.”

blocks.text: Must One Recite the Buddha Single-Mindedly Undisturbed in Order to Be Reborn

inline.s: Q: Must one recite the Buddha single-mindedly undisturbed in order to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?

A: Faith, vow, and upholding the Name with single-mindedness is a sufficient condition — not a necessary condition — for rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. That is, if in daily life one has accomplished faith, vow, and upholding the Name with single-mindedness, then at death one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; this the World-Honored One clearly teaches in the Amitābha Sutra spoken by the Buddha. Although in daily life one has not accomplished faith, vow, and upholding the Name with single-mindedness, if at death the right thought is clear and the Buddha's welcome is sensed, one will also be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Master Yinguang says: “One invokes with one's whole mind and spirit. Apart from this thought there is absolutely no other thought. Though one has not personally realized single-mindedness, yet in the end the mind is utterly without another thought.” (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · Reply to the Layman Chen Xinru.) Please note:
“Though one has not personally realized single-mindedness, yet in the end the mind is utterly without another thought.”
Nevertheless, looking at the cases of reciters of the Buddha being reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss across a thousand years, the number who succeed in this way is extremely small.

“This human body is hard to obtain and is now obtained; the Buddha-Dharma is hard to hear and is now heard. If this body is not delivered in this life, in what life shall it be delivered?” We have drifted in the sea of karma from the beginningless eons, now rising our heads, now sinking, having tasted all bitterness. How fortunate to have this incomparably sublime opportunity to hear the Buddha-Dharma and cultivate the Pure Land — how can we idly let this good chance slip away and vainly hope to win by luck? What's more, single-mindedness in reciting the Buddha is something everyone can attain through hard effort! This is why the World-Honored One again and again earnestly teaches: one must practice as taught. In the Sutra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha says:
“Though one toils painfully through a whole life, [the time is] but a moment; reborn in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, one enjoys bliss without limit.”
